query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Environment-assisted embrittlement during high-temperature exposure to reactive gases is governed by localized oxygen infiltration (or other reactive species) at grain and interphase boundaries within the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 fcc matrix, leading to the nucleation and growth of brittle secondary phases; these phases cause microcracks that coalesce under stress into catastrophic failure.
generation.material_initial_state: As-fabricated or solution-annealed Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with a single-phase fcc matrix.
generation.intervention: Perform in-situ high-temperature environmental TEM or synchrotron X-ray experiments under controlled oxygen partial pressures (e.g., 10^−5 to 10^−1 atm) while tracking real-time microstructure evolution, interfacial chemistry, and crack propagation under mechanical loading.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures ranging from approximately 800 °C to 1000 °C in oxidizing (O2-rich) or reducing environments, with systematically varied oxygen partial pressures, under moderate tensile or creep stresses.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of oxygen-enriched interfaces, precipitates, or secondary phases in the otherwise ductile fcc matrix, causing premature crack initiation and propagation.
generation.mechanism: At higher oxygen partial pressures, reactive species diffuse along boundaries and induce abrupt local phase transformations. The rapid formation of brittle phases and intergranular cracks reduces ductility, triggering sudden fracture once a threshold of microcrack coalescence is reached.
generation.predicted_outcome: Significant embrittlement and reduced ductility under oxidizing conditions compared to baseline inert or low-oxygen exposures. In particular, local crack formation is expected to accelerate, culminating in rapid failure when oxygen partial pressure crosses a critical level.
generation.baseline: Similar temperature and mechanical stress conditions in a vacuum or inert atmosphere, yielding minimal phase transformation and only minor cracking, if any, at grain or interphase boundaries.
generation.boundary: Oxygen partial pressures of 10^−5 atm or less should significantly reduce or delay degradation, while pressures up to 10^−1 atm are expected to trigger extensive oxide reactions and embrittlement within the alloy.
generation.uncertainty: Exact kinetics of boundary oxidation and the precise pressure-temperature thresholds for brittle phase nucleation remain uncertain and should be refined with in-situ experimental data.

falsification_experiment.design: Subject replicate specimens to identical thermal and mechanical loading in side-by-side trials under varying oxygen partial pressures (from 10^−5 to 10^−1 atm). Continuously monitor microstructural changes and crack evolution using in-situ imaging tools (e.g., environmental TEM) to detect the formation of brittle phases or lost ductility.
measurements: Microstructural evolution via real-time imaging (e.g., phase formation at boundaries and interfaces)
Local chemical composition to track oxygen infiltration
Tensile or creep deformation behaviors (stress–strain curves, elongation, time to failure)
Crack nucleation size, rate, and propagation under load
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples exposed to higher oxygen partial pressures do not display a marked increase in interface reactions, brittle phase formation, or sudden loss of ductility/strength compared to inert-exposed controls, the proposed mechanism of oxygen-driven embrittlement is falsified.

The bright-field TEM image in Fig. 2a demonstrates that the alloy is composed of an fcc matrix in which the hcp phase grows in the form of laminate with a thickness ranging from several to several hundred nanometers. High-resolution HAADF-STEM images of the hcp phase were taken along the fcc [110] direction (Fig. 2b), from which the coherent phase boundaries between the fcc and hcp phases can be observed. The interphase plane is represented by the close-packed planes of each structure: (111) for the fcc and (0001) for the hcp phase. No crystal defects, such as dislocations could be observed at these phase boundaries. Compared to other single-phase HEAs, the microstructure of this DP-HEA is significantly more complex. The hcp phase grows in the fcc matrix and, as such, serves to terminate slip planes for dislocation glide, thereby reducing the mean-free path for dislocation glide. AbstractHigh entropy alloys (HEAs) have demonstrated excellent potential in various applications owing to the unique properties. One of the most critical issues of HEAs is the stress corrosion cracking (SCC) which limits its reliability in practical applications. However, the SCC mechanisms have not been fully understood yet because of the difficulty of experimental measuring of atomic-scale deformation mechanisms and surface reactions. In this work, we conduct atomistic uniaxial tensile simulations using an FCC-type Fe40Ni40Cr20 alloy as a typical simplification of normal HEAs, in order to reveal how a corrosive environment such as high-temperature/pressure water affects the tensile behaviors and deformation mechanisms. In a vacuum, we observe the generation of layered HCP phases in an FCC matrix during tensile simulation induced by the formation of Shockley partial dislocations from surface and grain boundaries. While, in the corrosive environment of high-temperature/pressure water, the alloy surface is oxidized by chemical reactions with water and this oxide surface layer can suppress the formation of Shockley partial dislocation as well as the resulting FCC-to-HCP phase transit

decision.trend: Recent reactive-atomistic simulations of Fe–Ni–Cr-based high-entropy alloys highlight that high-temperature gaseous environments can drive surface reactions and induce phase transformations (e.g., a shift from HCP-dominated to BCC-dominated microstructures) differing greatly from inert or vacuum conditions. Under reactive conditions, surface oxide layers and embrittling secondary phases can form, which suppress typical slip or twinning and reduce ductility. These findings imply that environment-assisted embrittlement and altered slip or phase evolution lead to an increased propensity for sudden crack formation and thus catastrophic failure under oxidizing or reducing atmospheres.
decision.unsolved: It remains unclear how microstructural changes at and beneath the surface transition from benign to strongly embrittling, which specific pathways trigger intergranular or transgranular failure, and how to control the environment–alloy interactions to mitigate these failure modes. The critical local transformations and the synergy between local gas composition, temperature, and alloy microstructure require further mechanistic clarity.
decision.lever: Perform high-temperature environmental TEM or synchrotron X-ray experiments under controlled oxygen partial pressures (e.g., 10^−5 to 10^−1 atm) while tracking real-time microstructure evolution, interfacial chemistry, and crack propagation in the fcc matrix and interphase boundaries.
decision.why: This approach directly targets the role of reactive gases in promoting localized phase transformations and embrittlement at elevated temperatures. By correlating in situ observations of microstructural degradation with gas composition, one can identify the threshold conditions under which catastrophic failure initiates. Comparison to a vacuum or inert environment baseline will confirm whether newly formed phases and oxygen-driven boundary attacks indeed govern the rapid loss of structural integrity. If catastrophic fracture does not manifest under similar mechanical loading without the reactive gas environment, that will falsify the hypothesis that surface-induced oxidation is the critical trigger for sudden failure.
